title: Event-Driven Trading
answer: Event-driven trading in AI focuses on price moves that follow discrete, identifiable events such as merger announcements, litigation outcomes, and regulatory decisions. The site tracks 354 merger and acquisition filings and 148 active AI lawsuits, which are examples of the kind of events that can reprice AI-related instruments. Practitioners also watch earnings surprises, product launches, and changes in compliance rules. sections.body: Event-driven trading in AI focuses on price moves that follow discrete, identifiable events such as merger announcements, litigation outcomes, and regulatory decisions. The site tracks 354 merger and acquisition filings and 148 active AI lawsuits, which are examples of the kind of events that can reprice AI-related instruments. Practitioners also watch earnings surprises, product launches, and changes in compliance rules. The scope is narrower than broad market timing because the trade is tied to a specific catalyst with a known timeline.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on data feeds that capture filings, court dockets, regulatory registers, and news wires. For slower strategies, daily price series on the site's 117 listed AI-related instruments provide a baseline for measuring event impact. Low-latency setups add streaming market data, event detection engines, and text parsing pipelines. Storage and compute are typically cloud-based, with versioned datasets so that every event can be traced back to its source.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with an event taxonomy that defines which filings, rulings, or announcements matter for a given universe. Data is ingested, deduplicated, and parsed, often with natural language processing to extract entities, dates, and outcomes. Analysts then assess materiality and model an expected price range, using historical analogues and volatility estimates. Execution can be manual or automated, with position sizing and stop rules set before the event. Post-event review compares the realized move to the model and updates the taxonomy.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on data licensing, insider trading prohibitions, and market manipulation rules. Event data must have clear provenance, ideally from primary sources such as court dockets or regulatory filings, not from unverified social posts. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages and 148 active AI lawsuits show how much governance activity can surround AI instruments. Practitioners also manage operational risk from false positives, stale data, and execution failures.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward faster detection, more machine-readable sources, and tighter integration of event data with risk systems. Regulatory filings and court records are increasingly available in structured formats, which reduces parsing lag. At the same time, the volume of AI-related events, from lawsuits to compliance changes, is likely to keep growing. The site's 732 AI tools and 686 glossary terms reflect an expanding vocabulary that event-driven desks will need to track.
